novelty.justification: The idea directly extends the reference SB/NSGA-II approach: "Decompose multi-vessel COLREGS scene generation from *one* unconstrained problem into *P* class-anchored sub-problems". It fixes the paper's stated diversity/completeness failure, but the core search paradigm is unchanged. The class-targeting is a meaningful extension rather than a new paradigm.
novelty.rubric: Incremental: a meaningful extension or optimization of prior baseline work that fixes a concrete prior limitation, but the core paradigm is unchanged.
novelty.differentiation: Unlike R1/R3/R38/R40, which treat generation as essentially one unconstrained search/sampling problem and measure coverage post hoc, DCDG anchors one bounded NSGA-II run per COLREGS functional equivalence class and adds an explicit geometric-infeasibility report for residual classes.

feasibility.justification: The work is grounded in existing code and tools, with the idea stating it will "run bounded NSGA-II anchored to it" and reporting a prior "Pilot signal: POSITIVE — per-class hit 62.5%/87.5%". However, full validation across K=2..6, multiple baselines, per-class aggregation, and infeasibility reporting remains standard research engineering rather than near-zero effort.
feasibility.rubric: Moderate workload (sweet spot): needs nontrivial coding such as scripting existing open-source tools (parsers, CFG extractors) or building a custom graph-processing pipeline; standard research engineering effort.

clarity.justification: The plan is concrete: "Method thesis: enumerate classes → target each → aggregate → report feasibility"; "Protocol: K=2..6; SB (unconstrained baseline) vs RS (Scenic) vs CommonOcean AIS (CO), plus the new directed generator"; and all six metrics are named. Some exact hyperparameters and infeasibility-report criteria remain underspecified, but the proposal is actionable.
clarity.rubric: Clear and concrete: steps are explicit with a reasonable, specific experiment design (baseline tools, metric definitions); can be turned into a solid proposal.

notes: Scores the intermediate idea artifact (not the final paper).
Dimensions: novelty, feasibility, clarity (each 1-5). Excitement removed.
Novelty is scored against a Solution Space built from mineru REFERENCES titles (+ related_work.json abstracts when matched).
idea_generation.summary: DCDG proposes decomposing multi-vessel COLREGS scenario generation into per-functional-equivalence-class NSGA-II subproblems, unioning outputs, and reporting infeasible residual classes. It directly addresses the reference paper's known diversity/completeness collapse. The contribution is a plausible incremental extension of existing search-based maritime/automotive scenario generation rather than a new paradigm. Feasibility is moderate: there is a positive pilot and an existing toolkit, but the full K=2..6 evaluation remains standard research engineering. Clarity is good, with explicit metrics, baselines, and protocol, though some algorithmic details need refinement.
strengths: Directly targets the reference paper's stated future-work gap on diversity and completeness.
Empirically grounded pilot results, including a decisive builder-only ablation.
Clear metrics and baseline protocol from the reproduced paper.
weaknesses: Core search mechanism is an extension of existing NSGA-II scene generation rather than a new technique.
Exact per-class optimizer settings and infeasibility-report decision criteria are not fully specified.
Scalability beyond K=6 and sensitivity to class enumeration cost remain uncertain.

claims.statement: Test scenarios derived from real-world AIS/CommonOcean data are insufficient for testing multi-ship COLREGS-compliance encounters.

claims.evidence_quote: while rejection sampling was proven highly beneficial in the automotive domain, it was not effective in generating maritime test scenarios

claims.evidence_quote: synthetic test generation techniques repeatedly derived scenarios where the functional scenario model was inconsistent

original.overall_conclusion: Automotive scenario generation techniques can be adapted to maritime COLREGS testing, and search-based generation provides adequate speed and scalability, but both SB and RS have limited diversity and completeness for multi-vessel encounters. Real-world AIS-derived CommonOcean scenarios are largely insufficient for testing multi-ship COLREGS compliance due to low relevance and rare multi-vessel encounters.
original.comparable_notes: Experiments compare search-based (SB), rejection-sampling (RS), and CommonOcean AIS data. Measurements used 1000 runs per approach/problem size with a 10-minute timeout on Ubuntu 24.04, Intel Haswell, 32GB RAM, Python 3.12, reset seeds, garbage collection, and two warm-up runs. Scenes were abstracted with l2f into functional equivalence classes; relevance is measured by T∩C and ambiguity by A∩C, with ambiguity defined only for multi-vessel (K>2) scenarios.

claims.statement: DCDG improves functional equivalence-class coverage over search-based generation at every problem size K=2..6, reaching 73.0% versus 57.1% at K=6 and 94.3% versus 68.6% at K=5.

claims.statement: Naive random sampling from the class model is feasible only 0.000% of the time, so the search does the work.

agent.overall_conclusion: DCDG improves multi-vessel COLREGS scenario coverage by decomposing generation into class-anchored searches, reaching 100/100/97.1/94.3/73.0% coverage for K=2..6 versus SB 100/93.3/82.9/68.6/57.1% and avoiding rejection-sampling collapse (0% for K>=5). Ablations show naive random sampling is feasible only 0.000% of the time and a single unconstrained NSGA-II run collapses to at most one known class, supporting decomposition as the operative mechanism.
